name: microplans-study-groups
narrative: Maya wants to start a brand-new two-arm study, so she creates a new study on her existing Kaura programme. Maya clicks “+ Add a plan in the editor”, and in the plan UI she turns on the service-delivery data for the opportunity she's building the study around — a child health campaign. The visits blanket the whole of Attakar ward, showing where Connect has records of service delivery.  She decides she'll use the administrative boundaries — wards — as the survey units. Maya clicks on Attakar to select it and tags it as the intervention arm. Maya switches the plan to sampling mode and clicks "Compare surrounding boundaries". The tool finds every ward that shares a border with Attakar, measures each one's local building-density distribution, and ranks them by how closely that distribution overlaps Attakar's - filling each candidate's boundary on the map in its own colour so she can see which ward is which. The tightest match, Zankan, was the programme's ward last cycle — not a clean, un-treated control — so Maya skips it for Gura, the next-closest neighbour the programme never touched. One click of "Add boundary" on Gura's row adds it as the control arm; both wards now sit in one plan, each carrying its arm. She sets the sampling methodology — size-balanced PSU bands and a building-footprint-size filter — and clicks Generate plan. In one action the editor draws the sample for both arms and creates the plan. From the program workspace Maya can then send the plan to an existing locally led organization to verify if they are already under contact, or create a new solicitation from the plan for local organizations in the Connect network to apply to.

maya.name: Maya
maya.intro: Maya designs a controlled rooftop-survey impact study for the Kaura Vitamin-A programme and needs two comparable arms that field surveyors execute completely blind.

slides.title: Maya starts a study from scratch
slides.narration: Maya starts a brand-new two-arm study on her Kaura programme.

slides.title: Maya opens the plan editor on the empty study
slides.narration: In the plan editor she turns on the campaign's service-delivery data.

slides.title: Maya sees the programme covered all of Attakar
slides.narration: The visits blanket Attakar — everywhere Connect logged delivery. She'll sample by ward.

slides.title: Maya compares the surrounding wards to find a control
slides.narration: She tags Attakar as the intervention arm and runs Compare. Every neighbouring ward is ranked against it — but look at what the table shows. Match is how similar the two wards look overall. The column that matters is Matched balance: if Maya picks this ward as her control and lets the engine match-sample it, how balanced the two arms actually come out — the very number her study's comparability check will report. And Common support is how much of the settlement-density range the two wards share, because matching only draws from that shared range. So a ward that's only a partial overall match can still deliver a perfectly balanced study.

slides.title: Maya rejects the closest match and adds the right control
slides.narration: Sopp and Gura are the best-balanced controls, both at 0.02. Zankan was the programme's own ward last cycle, so it's out. Of the two, Gura shares more common support with Attakar — so Maya makes it the control arm.

slides.title: Maya generates the two-arm plan in place
slides.narration: She sets the sampling methodology and clicks Generate — both arms' sample drawn in one pass, balanced by design.

slides.title: Maya completes the study
slides.narration: She advances the plan to Approved. Each area keeps its arm labs-side and the Connect export carries no arm column, so surveyors stay blind. The study's ready to hand to a survey firm.
